claims.text: High-temperature oxidation resistance in multiprincipal-element refractory alloys is controlled by formation of a continuous protective mixed-oxide scale.
Material integrity during high-temperature oxidation is controlled by formation of a continuous protective mixed-oxide scale.
Reactive elements such as Hf or Cr preferentially segregate to grain boundaries and alloy surfaces at high temperature.
Reactive-element segregation promotes nucleation of slow-growing, adherent oxides.
The resulting oxides act as a barrier to oxygen diffusion.
The proposed initial alloy is homogeneous and has a nominally uniform elemental distribution.
Current refractory high-entropy-alloy studies include multiprincipal W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf compositions containing both Cr and Hf.
The alloy has the potential to develop reactive-element segregation under thermal activation.
The alloy's intrinsic chemical complexity drives selective segregation of reactive elements to grain boundaries and surfaces.
Local reactive-element enrichment facilitates formation of a continuous and adherent mixed-oxide layer.
A continuous mixed-oxide scale slows oxygen diffusion into the alloy bulk.
Slower oxygen diffusion limits continued oxidation and mitigates oxidation-induced degradation.
Alloys engineered for stronger reactive-element segregation will form thinner, more uniform, and slower-growing oxide scales than a baseline with weaker segregation.
Stronger reactive-element segregation will produce lower oxidation weight gain than the baseline.
Stronger reactive-element segregation will improve preservation of mechanical integrity after oxidation.
An alloy with less reactive-element segregation or lower Hf/Cr content will form a less protective oxide scale under otherwise identical conditions.
The proposed governing behavior should hold at approximately 1000–1300 K under moderate oxygen partial pressures.
The proposed mechanism may cease to govern when alternative oxidation mechanisms dominate or rapid scale spallation occurs.
